hints: Focus on the two separate clues here, the colour of the silver halide precipitate and what happens in concentrated ammonia.
Remember that $\text{AgI}$ is yellow and stays solid even in concentrated ammonia, while $\text{AgCl}$ is white and $\text{AgBr}$ is cream to pale yellow.
Think about what mixture would look pale yellow at first but leave only a darker yellow solid after part of it dissolves away.
walkthrough:
**Recall the colours of the silver halides**

This is the classic test for halides. Think colour first.

$$\text{AgCl is white, AgBr is cream or pale yellow, AgI is yellow}$$

**Recall solubility in ammonia**

Ammonia dissolves the precipitates by forming a complex ion, but the darker halides hold on more strongly.

$$\text{AgCl dissolves in dilute } \text{NH}_3, \text{ AgBr dissolves only in concentrated } \text{NH}_3, \text{ AgI is insoluble even in concentrated } \text{NH}_3$$

**Use the partly dissolving observation**

Part dissolves and part remains. So we must have two precipitates present.

The residue is darker yellow and survives concentrated ammonia, so it must be $\text{AgI}$. That tells us iodide was in the powder.

**Explain the pale initial colour**

$\text{AgI}$ alone would be distinctly yellow and would not dissolve at all.

Here the first precipitate is paler yellow and partly dissolves. That fits a mixture of white $\text{AgCl}$ plus yellow $\text{AgI}$ looking pale yellow together, then the white $\text{AgCl}$ dissolves in ammonia to leave the darker yellow $\text{AgI}$ behind.

options.A: Sodium bromide only would give cream or pale yellow $\text{AgBr}$. This would dissolve completely in concentrated ammonia, leaving no darker yellow residue, so it cannot match the observation.
options.B: Sodium iodide only would give yellow $\text{AgI}$. This is insoluble even in concentrated ammonia, so the precipitate would not partly dissolve at all.
options.C: A mixture of chloride and bromide would give white $\text{AgCl}$ plus cream $\text{AgBr}$. Both dissolve in concentrated ammonia ($\text{AgCl}$ even in dilute), so everything would dissolve and no yellow residue would remain.
options.D: A mixture of chloride and iodide gives white $\text{AgCl}$ plus yellow $\text{AgI}$, which together appear pale yellow. On adding concentrated ammonia, the $\text{AgCl}$ dissolves away, leaving the insoluble darker yellow $\text{AgI}$. This matches both observations perfectly.
